misconception_diagnosis.justification: Turn 1 immediately and precisely diagnoses the TH3 'metal is inherently cold' misconception, validating the observation while reframing it: 'you're not measuring its temperature directly — you're measuring how quickly heat is transferred,' attributing the sensation to thermal conductivity and invoking thermal equilibrium so both objects share room temperature. Names the misconception, validates the experience, and corrects the conclusion.

scaffolding_strategy.justification: Turn 1 uses a well-structured Socratic sequence (does 'feels colder' mean colder? same room -> same temperature? what if it feels colder anyway?) appropriate to the level, and follows the student's own extension questions (glass, water, ice, ceramic). The tutor stays responsive and level-matched, though it answers each new sub-question fairly fully rather than continuing to elicit, so 3.

answer_disclosure_restraint.justification: Turn 1 holds back well with genuine questions, but turn 2 gives the complete answer ('both at the same temperature... metal feels colder due to high thermal conductivity'). Mostly guides initially but tells at the key moment, so 2.

conceptual_model_building.justification: Builds a robustly transferable model: sensation tracks RATE of heat flow (conductivity), not temperature; objects sharing an environment reach equilibrium at equal temperature; with a clear conductivity ordering (metal>ice>water>glass>plastic) and the boundary case (when actual temperatures differ, temperature dominates). Connects to many materials and notes when each factor governs.

transfer_success.justification: The transfer (metal vs plastic ice tray from the same freezer, why metal feels painfully colder) is posed at turn 7. The student's turn-8 reply answers correctly and independently: 'both at the same temperature (the freezer temperature), but the metal feels much colder because it conducts heat away from my skin faster,' and generalizes to railings/spoons. Clean independent transfer.

pedagogical_harm_avoidance.justification: Physics is correct throughout (thermal equilibrium, conductivity-driven sensation, correct conductivity ranking; the tutor even catches the impossible 'ice at 20 C' premise). It consistently validates the student's observations and reasoning and keeps a warm, encouraging tone. Actively confidence-building and safe.
